title: Ghana Macroeconomic Dashboard
text:
Ghana’s economy sits at a fascinating intersection of colonial history, commodity dependence, and recurring IMF intervention. This project explores how key macroeconomic indicators — GDP, inflation, interest rates, exchange rates, and commodity prices — have evolved since independence, and what their relationships reveal about the structural dynamics of a developing economy.
The final product is an interactive Shiny dashboard that allows users to explore these indicators visually and run their own Granger Causality tests to investigate lead-lag relationships between variables.
Tools used: R, Shiny, ggplot2, Ghana Statistical Service, Bank of Ghana data

title: Ghana Macroeconomic Dashboard
text:
Key Question

Ghana has relied on IMF bailouts in 1966, the 1970s, 1980s, 1990s, 2009, 2015, and 2022. Each intervention coincides with periods of currency depreciation, rising inflation, and commodity price shocks. But do these patterns follow conventional economic theory — or does Ghana’s developing economy behave differently?

title: Ghana Macroeconomic Dashboard
text:
Data & Methodology
Data was sourced from the Ghana Statistical Service and the Bank of Ghana, arriving in inconsistent monthly formats across multiple Excel files. A custom R cleaning pipeline standardized date formats, removed formatting artifacts, handled missing values, and converted all monthly series into annual averages. Year-over-year (YoY) transformations were calculated for key variables including inflation, exchange rates, gold prices, GDP, monetary supply, cocoa prices, and oil prices — because YoY changes highlight turning points and accelerations that raw levels obscure.
Granger Causality was chosen over standard regression because the core economic questions involve lead-lag relationships: does inflation predict future policy rate decisions? Do commodity prices lead exchange rate movements? Granger testing is specifically designed to answer these questions.

title: Ghana Macroeconomic Dashboard
text:
Key Findings
Inflation and monetary policy move together, with a lag. During periods of economic stress (2009, 2015, 2022), inflation spiked and the Bank of Ghana responded by raising its policy rate — which in turn pushed up commercial lending rates. The dashboard makes this lagged relationship visible and testable.
Cocoa and the cedi are linked — but gold is different. When the cedi depreciates, Ghanaian farmers earn more cedis per dollar exported, incentivizing oversupply on the world market and pushing cocoa prices down. Gold, however, behaves as global money driven by US dollar strength, geopolitical risk, and global inflation expectations — not Ghanaian supply dynamics. A Granger Causality test on gold prices vs. the cedi returned a p-value of 0.1757, indicating gold does not show clear predictive power for the cedi once its own past is controlled for.
IMF interventions are visible but hard to isolate. The 2009, 2015, and 2022 bailout periods all coincide with currency instability and rising inflation, but isolating the precise effect of each program is difficult given the extended duration of interventions and the confounding effects of global commodity shocks.

title: Ghana Macroeconomic Dashboard
text:
Reflection
This project reinforced that macroeconomic relationships in developing economies rarely follow textbook predictions cleanly. Ghana’s heavy dependence on gold, cocoa, and oil exposes it to global price shocks outside its control, while recurring IMF engagement reflects structural challenges that short-term stabilization programs cannot fully resolve. Future extensions would incorporate higher-frequency monthly or weekly data to capture short-run dynamics that annual averages smooth out.
